Where it began

Sunil Gavaskar was born in Bombay on 10 July 1949. Cricket ran in the family: his mother's brother, Madhav Mantri, had kept wicket for India, and his sister Kavita later married the Test batsman Gundappa Viswanath. At school he piled up runs so freely that in 1966 he was named the country's best schoolboy cricketer.

His first Ranji Trophy match for Bombay brought a duck. He answered with a hundred against Rajasthan in his second game, then two more in a row, and the selectors put him on the plane to the West Indies.

The player

Few careers have started like it. In that 1971 series in the Caribbean he made 774 runs in four Tests, a record for anyone's first series, and hit the winning runs in India's first ever Test victory over the West Indies. In the final Test at Port of Spain he made a hundred and a double hundred in the same match. A calypso was written in his honour.

He played 125 Tests between 1971 and 1987 and made 10,122 runs at 51.12, with 34 hundreds and a best of 236 not out. He was the first batsman in history to pass 10,000 Test runs, and for many years nobody had made more Test hundreds. He also played 106 Tests in a row, and captained India in 47 of his matches.

What made him special

Gavaskar faced the great West Indian fast bowlers of his era with a straight bat, a steady head and endless patience, and against them he made 2,749 runs with 13 hundreds. Imran Khan called him the most compact batsman he ever bowled to. When the moment asked for it he could attack too: against Malcolm Marshall in Delhi he hooked his way to a half-century in 37 balls. He was a safe catcher at slip as well, the first Indian outfielder to hold a hundred Test catches.

The one-day game was a slower friendship. He waited until almost his last match to make a one-day hundred, and when it came, against New Zealand at the 1987 World Cup, it took him only 88 balls. Clearly he had been saving it.

Away from the middle

After his playing days he became one of the best-known voices in the commentary box and a long-serving newspaper columnist. He wrote several books, Sunny Days among them, starred in a Marathi film and even recorded a song comparing life to a game of cricket.

The honours came steadily: the Arjuna Award, the Padma Bhushan, Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1980, a place in cricket's Hall of Fame in 2009 and the C. K. Nayudu award for a lifetime in the game. He served a year as the honorary Sheriff of Bombay, and the series between India and Australia is played for the Border–Gavaskar Trophy.

And finally

In 2017 a cricket ground in Louisville, Kentucky, was named after him, and the mayor handed him the keys. For a man who spent sixteen years refusing to give his wicket away, it seems only fair that someone finally gave him something to keep.
